name: Hair dryer brush (hot air brush)

card.summary: Brush-dryer hybrid for volume and quick blowouts; claims come from product reviews, with no clinical studies.
card.aka: hair dryer brush, blow-dry brush, Revlon One-Step
card.note: Sources are consumer reviews; no clinical studies on volume or hair damage.

quick.overview:
A hot air brush is a brush with heated airflow built in, so hair is dried and styled at once. It is promoted for root lift and volume, especially on fine hair.

The claims come from product testers, and no clinical studies were found.
quick.mechanism: A motor blows heated air through the brush head while bristles lift and shape hair, drying and smoothing it in one step.
quick.risks: No device-specific safety research was found; the main consideration is heat exposure to hair and scalp, as with other heated styling tools.

lead: A hot air brush, also called a hair dryer brush or blow-dry brush, is a handheld styling tool that combines a brush with heated airflow so hair can be dried, smoothed and given volume in a single pass. People use it to get a salon-style blowout at home: lifted roots, body, a smoother finish and more shine, usually in less time than a separate dryer and round brush.[1][2]

Wikipedia's hair dryer article describes the hair dryer brush as a brush-shaped dryer used for volume, available in rotating and static versions.[2] Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, says oval heads tend to build root lift and volume while round heads suit shorter hair and sleek finishes, and that the tools are used especially for body on fine or thin hair. Popular models it names include the Revlon One-Step Volumizer Plus 2.0 and the Dyson Airwrap.[1]

The device draws air over a heating element and out through vents in the brush head while the bristles lift and direct hair. No published clinical studies of hot air brushes were found; descriptions come from reference sources and product reviews.[1][2]

chain: Brush bristles lift hair at the roots while heated air dries it
Hair sets with lift, smoothness and shine
Fuller, groomed-looking hair for the day
angle.text: The tool lets users dry and shape hair in one step, giving root lift and a smooth finish that makes fine or flat hair look fuller. It is used for quick blowouts before work, events or photos.

infobox: Ionic function, ceramic or tourmaline barrels, adjustable heat, cool shot[1][2]
Integral immersion protection required on US hand-held hair dryers[1]

paras: Grokipedia describes a motor drawing air over a heating element and expelling it through vents in a barrel-shaped brush head, with bristles lifting and separating strands as the user glides the brush through hair.[1] Some models add ionic technology, said by manufacturers to reduce static and frizz, and some offer rotating barrels or multiple attachments.[1] Wikipedia's article on hair dryers notes that ionic settings are meant to reduce static but that their effectiveness is debated, and that a cool shot button blows room-temperature air to help set a style.[2]

Feature lists in the Grokipedia entry cover brush shape (oval for lift, round for smooth finishes), barrel material (ceramic, titanium, tourmaline), heat and airflow settings, attachments, and budget, with premium models adding Coanda airflow.[1]

Grokipedia dates hot air brushes to the late twentieth century as a way to combine a blow dryer and round brush, with mid-1990s patents describing a handle-mounted blower feeding a brush head with vents.[1] Ionic technology became common from the 2010s, and Dyson's 2018 Airwrap introduced Coanda airflow, which shapes hair with less direct heat.[1] The wider hair dryer dates to Alexandre Godefroy's 1888 salon device, with handheld household models appearing around 1920.[2]

Claims about volume, time savings and less heat damage than flat irons come from product testers and manufacturers, whom Grokipedia lists as including Good Housekeeping, Allure, WIRED and others.[1] Testers cited there report faster drying than a separate dryer and round brush.[1] No independent study measuring these outcomes was found.

Wikipedia's article on hair straightening says that too much heat or heat applied for too long can permanently alter hair structure, that protective sprays can reduce the risk, and that low or medium heat settings protect hair and scalp during blow-drying.[3] Grokipedia says airflow-based tools generally create fewer hot spots than flat irons, advises the lowest effective heat for fine or damaged hair, and notes burn and electrical risks if the unit is touched while hot or falls in water.[1] Wikipedia reports that US dryers have been required to include a ground fault circuit interrupter since 1991.[2]

timeline.event: Alexandre Godefroy invents the first hair dryer.[2]
Early patents describe a handle-mounted blower feeding a vented brush head.[1]
Ionic technology becomes common in hot air brushes.[1]
Dyson introduces the Airwrap with Coanda airflow.[1]
